episodes.216237: Episodic rounds of strong thunderstorms plagued northeast Kentucky on August 11st amid a long stretch of active weather that prevailed over the bulk of the country. The first round of the day took shape during the late morning hours, casting a cluster of downed trees and power lines in parts of Greenup County. Atmospheric recovery efforts quickly got underway once the first round of storms dashed east of the state line, with the next round hot on its tracks for the afternoon. Convection upstream featured  a corridor of severe strength storms stretching from Central Indiana into the Columbus area of Ohio and tracking south-southeastward. Storms followed the path of least resistance when it came to their propagation through the Ohio Valley, reaching northeast Kentucky once again during the peak of the afternoon. Another swath of downed trees and power lines ensued before activity departed once more for West Virginia. While a warm front remained parked within the vicinity of the Ohio Valley and Central Appalachians, this active weather pattern was about to thrive.

episodes.217438: During the afternoon and evening hours of August 11th, multiple bowing segments developed and moved over central Kentucky and southern Indiana from northwest to southeast. The mid-afternoon wave was from a derecho that had originated in eastern Iowa during the early morning hours of August 11, moving through northern Illinois, Indiana, and Ohio before entering our forecast area. This wave was also at the nose of a 40-50 kt 500 mb jet that was producing 30-50 kt of deep layer shear. There was also ample atmospheric moisture in place, with PW values over 1.8. Considerable severe wind gusts and damage was experienced across north central Kentucky and southeastern Indiana, highlighted by an 81 mph wind gust at the Nicholas County Mesonet site. Another bowing segment would develop in eastern Illinois/western Indiana and travel southeast along the outflow boundary left by the initial system. Favorable environmental conditions allowed for scattered areas of wind damage to occur in southern Indiana and north central Kentucky. With the high moisture in place as well as additional development of showers and thunderstorms over south central Kentucky, some places that experienced repeated rounds of rainfall experienced some flash flooding. A round of repeated showers and storms occurred during the late overnight/early morning hours of the 12th. A few smaller bowing segments did develop that produced some brief damaging winds, however the persistent rainfall that lasted through most of the morning hours resulted in flash flooding for some places east of I-65. A line of showers and thunderstorms moved through southern Indiana and central Kentucky during the afternoon and early evening hours of the 12th, as well as a few isolated showers and storms over south central Kentucky. While environmental parameters were not as favorable given the repeated rounds of showers and storms, higher instability was in place over portions of central Kentucky that produced isolated areas of thunderstorm wind damage.

episodes.218255: Several severe thunderstorms affected western South Dakota on August 11th, 2026, including two particularly destructive and long-track supercells. One produced giant hail (up to 4 in diameter), and the other produced extreme winds (up to 111 MPH).||Giant Hail Producer (started in the Black Hills)|This long-track thunderstorm, and prolific and destructive hail producer, formed just after 1:00 PM MDT in the northern Black Hills. The storm initially sat over this area, shedding updrafts off its northern flank and struggling to move off the hills. It then matured into a supercell and started moving southeast, producing numerous reports of quarter (1.0��� diameter) to tennis ball size (2.50��� diameter) hail from near Nemo, to near Johnson Siding, to near Rockerville. Hail covered the ground and resulted in numerous broken windshields in the Rockerville area. The storm continued southeast experiencing several mergers, impacting the Hayward to Hermosa corridor with numerous reports of baseball (2.75��� diameter) and larger sized hail, with the largest received measurement coming in at 3.6��� diameter 2 miles south-southwest of Hermosa measured by a storm chaser. The hail fell for 10-15 minutes in some areas! Shattered home and vehicle windows, dented vehicles, broken downspouts and gutters, and a destroyed carport were reported in this corridor. In far southeastern Custer County, a reliable storm spotter reported a short-lived, long rope funnel from the storm. As the storm tracked through Oglala Lakota County, a swath of baseball (2.75��� diameter) to 4.00��� diameter hail was reported across the Oglala and Pine Ridge areas, causing widespread and catastrophic damage to homes, vehicles, and gardens/vegetation. Numerous home and vehicle windows were smashed out, and roofs were damaged. A school district in Oglala was forced to delay the start of their school year due to significant damage to 26 of their vehicles, including their entire fleet of 10 school buses. This storm exited South Dakota just before 7:00 PM MDT and would go on to produce more 3.5��� hail through north-central Nebraska.||Extreme Wind Producer (started in southeast Montana)|This destructive, long-track thunderstorm formed in far southeastern Montana, quickly becoming severe before moving into Harding County just after 4:00 PM MDT. The storm evolved into a high-impact, high-precipitation (HP) supercell for the first part of its lifespan tracking southeast across western South Dakota, producing damaging hail as large as baseballs (2.75��� diameter) and knocking down power poles between Camp Crook and Harding, and then intensifying and producing destructive winds ranging from 61 MPH to 111 MPH (13 miles northeast of Newell) across Butte County. Tree and structural damage was reported near Castle Rock. As the storm reached Meade County, the supercell structure deteriorated as more convection formed on its northeastern flank and the system started to elongate into more of a linear mode. It produced wind gusts to 79 MPH 3 miles northwest of Wasta, 84 MPH 2 miles east of Cottonwood, and 102 MPH 4 miles east of Cactus Flat as it reached the Interstate 90 corridor in Pennington and Jackson counties. Multiple vehicles including semi trailers were reported blown over along Interstate 90 near Wasta and Kadoka. Half-dollar size hail (1.25��� diameter) was also reported near Cedar Pass. Finally, the storm fully expanded/transitioned into a line as it continued to track southeast across Jackson, Mellette, Todd, and Tripp counties, producing widespread and significant wind damage. Wind gusts reached 83 MPH 4 miles west-northwest of Cedar Butte, 96 MPH 1 mile south of White River, 90 MPH 7 miles east-southeast of Rosebud, and 83 MPH in Wewela. Damage in Cedar Butte, White River, Mission, Rosebud, and Okreek included structural damage, outbuildings blown over, numerous trees snapped and uprooted, and windows blown out of homes and vehicles. The fairgrounds cook shack building in Rosebud collapsed, and the Tokala Inajinyo Youth Leadership Mentoring Program Resource Center 6 miles north-northeast of Rosebud was destroyed. Roofs were partially or completely blown off of multiple residences and businesses, and others had holes due to tree limb punctures. Per KELO-TV, severe wind damage rendered at least 53 homes uninhabitable across the Rosebud Reservation. North of Rosebud, an RV was blown over and rolled 50 feet, seriously injuring 1 person who was trapped inside and had to be cut out by firefighters. 78 power poles were also reported down or damaged across Mellette County. The storm exited into Nebraska by 1:00 AM CDT and continued to produce 60+ MPH wind gusts through northeast and eastern Nebraska.

Jay County Emergency Management found a narrow damage path through a mature soybean crop as they were traveling on S 350 E in extreme southern Jay County. This crop damage seemed to be going from NW to SE. An original short EF-U tornado was designated as there was originally no evidence of this tornado hitting one of the designated damage indicators. Due to improving weather, emergency management was able to get their drone up and found clear evidence that the tornado began farther to the northwest in another field of crops. It traversed southeast, coming very close to a property which is located along the county boundary. It is in this area that the tornado was likely the widest and most intense based on crop damage. It then crossed S 300 E and continued southeast. It appears to have struck a small cluster of trees where it broke several large limbs, earning the designation of an EF-0. It quickly terminated after that before reaching the county boundary road. Special thanks to Jay County's Office of Emergency Management for the assistance in documenting this storm.

The tornado began on South 8th Street between East Morrill Avenue and East Hinman Avenue, where it downed and uprooted several trees. Siding and roof damage occurred to several residences farther east toward Parsons Avenue, while a business lost a substantial amount of its roof on the east side of Parsons Avenue. Tree and mostly light structural damage continued to the east between East Hinman Avenue and Woodrow Avenue as the tornado moved east of Barack Park and damaged numerous trees and homes along and east of South Champion Avenue to Lockbourne Road. Reeb Avenue was particularly hard hit by the tornado's damaging winds before it crossed Lockbourne Road and damaged more trees in conjunction with multiple businesses. Additional trees and homes were impacted west of Fairwood Avenue, including the roof of one home that caved in due to fallen trees, along with significant damage to a metal roof of a business. The tornado ended just west of Fairwood Avenue.

After crossing the Olentangy River, additional tree damage was observed on North High Street and a few businesses sustained damage that included minor roof damage and broken windows. The tornado then followed Glen Echo Creek eastward and caused damage to trees along the creek and Olentangy Street. Several homes were damaged by the trees. As the tornado moved in a more northeast direction, additional tree damage was observed along U.S. Route 23 and in surrounding neighborhoods. As the tornado approached Interstate 71, minor roof damage was observed to a building along Silver Drive. Video from an ODOT traffic camera then observed the tornado crossing Interstate 71 at the Weber Road exit, where it flipped a single vehicle. Tree damage and minor home damage was next found on Beulah Road and East Weber Road. The tornado likely dissipated near this location.

The tornado then tracked farther to the southeast, resulting in additional spotty damage before more significant damage was observed in the vicinity of Chapel Road. Numerous large trees were snapped or uprooted along Chapel Road near the intersection with Jenkins Road, with some damage to structures due to fallen trees. Once in Hamilton County, sporadic tree damage occurred within a largely inaccessible area of the Fernald Preserve, with spotty isolated damage farther to the southeast. It is possible the tornado briefly lifted in the vicinity of Willey Road toward New Haven Road before more significant tree damage was observed on either side of the Great Miami River into the area of the Oak Glen Preserve. Although sporadic tree damage was reported southeast of the Oak Glen Preserve, the nature of the damage in conjunction with radar data, would suggest that the tornado dissipated at 1425EST.
